# **Kinetic Formation, Structural Architecture, and Physical Impacts of High-Molecular-Weight Melanoidins in Extruded Plant Proteins**

## **Introduction to Thermomechanical Polymerization in Plant Matrices**

The transition of globally available plant proteins into highly structured, anisotropic matrices capable of mimicking the exact physiological and rheological properties of animal muscle fiber relies heavily on the engineering principles of high-moisture extrusion (HME) and textured vegetable protein (TVP) processing. Within the thermodynamic confines of a twin-screw extruder, native globular plant proteins—most notably soy protein isolate (SPI) and pea protein isolate (PPI)—are subjected to extreme, compounding physical forces. These include intense mechanical shear, elevated barrel temperatures frequently exceeding 150 °C, and meticulously controlled feed moisture levels ranging from 20% to 57%.1 This highly energized environment effectively acts as a continuous thermochemical bioreactor. The application of specific mechanical energy (SME) systematically denatures the complex quaternary and tertiary structures of storage proteins, unwinding the 7S ![][image1]\-conglycinin and 11S glycinin fractions in soy, as well as the vicilin and legumin fractions in pea, into extended polypeptide chains.4  
However, the extrusion process is not purely a physical reorganization of native proteins; it is an environment that catalyzes profound and irreversible chemical modifications. Chief among these modifications is the Maillard reaction. Driven by the high thermal energy and intense shear, the extrusion conditions trigger the partial hydrolysis of residual polysaccharides and starch dextrinization, thereby liberating reactive reducing sugars directly into the plasticized protein melt.1 Concurrently, the mechanical unfolding of the protein networks exposes previously buried nucleophilic amino acid side chains, particularly the ![][image2]\-amino groups of lysine and the guanidino groups of arginine.5 The initial condensation between these carbonyl and amino groups sparks a complex cascade of chemical rearrangements, fragmentations, and polymerizations that culminate in the late stages of the Maillard reaction.  
The terminal phase of this non-enzymatic browning cascade is characterized by the generation of high-molecular-weight (HMW) melanoidins. Melanoidins are highly complex, nitrogen-containing, heterogeneous polymers that possess an intricate, largely insoluble architecture.7 Historically relegated in the literature to mere browning agents evaluated through simplistic spectrophotometric absorbance readings, advanced macromolecular analysis now reveals that these HMW melanoidins function as critical, active structural cross-linkers within the plant protein extrudate. Their kinetic formation fundamentally alters the rheological parameters, hydration kinetics, and macroscopic texturization phase transitions of the resulting biopolymer networks.9 Furthermore, the dense, electron-rich molecular skeletons of these melanoidins possess a unique and highly aggressive chemical reactivity. They act as potent scavengers for the very flavor compounds required to create organoleptically viable food products, specifically trapping small, odor-active volatile thiols such as 2-methyl-3-furanthiol.11 Consequently, understanding the structural and physical impacts of melanoidins requires a rigorous, multi-disciplinary approach that synthesizes non-linear reaction kinetics, absolute macromolecular quantification, non-Newtonian rheology, and advanced quantitative flavor chemistry.

## **The Biochemical Cascade: Kinetic Formation of High-Molecular-Weight Melanoidins**

To understand the profound physical impacts of melanoidins on the extruded protein matrix, one must first deconstruct the exact chemical kinetics governing their formation under the uniquely harsh conditions of high-moisture extrusion. The Maillard reaction is classically divided into three distinct stages: early, advanced, and final. During the extrusion of SPI and PPI, the rapid heat transfer and high mechanical shear drastically accelerate the early and advanced stages, propelling the matrix almost immediately into the final stages of polymerization.1  
The early stage initiates with the nucleophilic attack of the exposed primary amino groups of lysine or arginine on the reactive carbonyl groups of reducing sugars, leading to the formation of a Schiff base. This inherently unstable intermediate rapidly undergoes an Amadori rearrangement (in the case of aldoses) or a Heyns rearrangement (in the case of ketoses) to yield relatively stable ketoamines.6 However, within the active cooking zone of the extruder barrel, where temperatures typically exceed 110 °C, these Amadori products are rapidly degraded. The degradation pathways are highly dependent on the localized pH of the melt and the available thermal energy. They undergo dehydration and fission to form highly reactive intermediate ![][image3]\-dicarbonyl compounds, such as glyoxal, methylglyoxal, 1-deoxyosones, and 3-deoxyosones.6  
It is during the advanced and final stages that the foundations of the melanoidin polymer are constructed. The ![][image3]\-dicarbonyls function as highly aggressive cross-linking agents. They engage in further reactions with additional free amino acids in the protein melt via Strecker degradation, releasing volatile aldehydes and generating intermediate pyrazines and pyrroles.14 More critically for the structural integrity of the extrudate, these dicarbonyls react directly with multiple amino acid side chains simultaneously, forming complex advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) that bridge adjacent protein chains. For example, the reaction of glyoxal or methylglyoxal with two lysine residues yields massive bis(lysyl)imidazolium cross-links, such as glyoxal-derived lysine dimer (GOLD) and methylglyoxal-derived lysine dimer (MOLD).6 Similarly, the involvement of arginine leads to the formation of cross-linked structures like pentosidine and complex colored melanoidin precursors such as BISARG.6  
The kinetic rate of this polymerization is heavily influenced by the specific parameters of the extrusion system. Kinetic modeling of the Maillard reaction during the covalent conjugation of soy proteins suggests that the macroscopic accumulation of these complex HMW melanoidin polymers actually follows pseudo-zero-order chemical kinetics under steady-state extrusion.3 This pseudo-zero-order behavior is a phenomenon directly attributed to the continuous, steady-state generation of highly reactive intermediate precursors under constant thermomechanical flux.3 As long as the mechanical shear continues to unfold proteins to expose new lysine residues, and the thermal energy continues to drive the dehydration of sugars, the polymerization rate remains constant, limited only by the residence time within the extruder barrel. Conversely, the denaturation of the native plant proteins themselves—such as the heat inactivation of trypsin inhibitors (TIA) during continuous processing—follows strict first-order reaction kinetics, demonstrating an activation energy of approximately 34 kJ/mol.15 This kinetic divergence highlights a critical processing reality: the physical unfolding of the protein matrix (first-order) occurs rapidly, while the subsequent chemical fixation and cross-linking via melanoidin formation (zero-order) proceeds steadily throughout the remainder of the extrusion timeline.  
The resulting HMW melanoidins are not uniform. They are highly polydisperse, heavily cross-linked co-polymers consisting of repeating furan, pyrrole, and pyrazine rings covalently tethered to the backbones of the soy or pea proteins.8 As the temperature in the final die zone increases, the molecular weight of the forming melanoidins increases exponentially, allowing them to function structurally akin to a thermosetting resin.10 Once this dense, rigid network is formed, it exhibits irreversible curing behavior; it does not remelt upon cooling, thereby providing the permanent structural stability that defines the final texture of the extrudate.10

## **Absolute Quantification Strategies: Overcoming the Browning Index**

Historically, the evaluation of the Maillard reaction in food matrices has heavily relied on simplistic colorimetric methods, most notably measuring the spectrophotometric absorbance of aqueous extracts at 420 nm or 470 nm to determine a "browning index." While these optical measurements provide a rudimentary assessment of the presence of colored compounds, they are woefully inadequate for the rigorous physical chemistry required to understand plant protein texturization. Lightness (![][image4]) and browning indices in a solid food matrix are highly susceptible to optical scattering caused by internal pore expansion, the inherent pigmentation of the raw isolates, and the crystallinity of the protein matrix.1 Consequently, modern analytical chemistry demands the exact quantitative measurement of the physical mass, absolute concentration, and molecular weight distribution of the formed melanoidin polymers.  
To isolate the true high-molecular-weight fraction of melanoidins and separate them from unreacted precursors, short-chain peptides, and low-molecular-weight Maillard intermediates, rigorous dialysis and ultrafiltration protocols are mandatory. Dialysis utilizing regenerated cellulose membranes with highly specific molecular weight cut-offs (MWCO)—typically retaining compounds with a molecular mass greater than 3,500 Daltons or 10,000 Daltons—ensures that only the true polymeric structures are retained for analysis.16  
To determine the absolute mass of the melanoidins generated, researchers have successfully employed radiochemical tracking utilizing ![][image5]\-labeled precursors. By introducing highly specific tracers, such as ![][image6]\-glycine or ![][image5]\-labeled glucose, into the model formulations prior to thermomechanical processing, the exact carbon skeleton of the precursors can be traced.17 Following extraction and dialysis of the extrudate, the residual radioactivity within the non-dialyzable high-molecular-weight fraction is measured. This method allows for the absolute quantification of the melanoidin mass incorporated into the protein network, proving that a significant proportion of the initial reducing sugars are permanently integrated into the HMW macromolecular structure.18  
For structural elucidation and the determination of absolute molecular weight distributions, High-Performance Size-Exclusion Chromatography (HPSEC) coupled with multi-angle laser light scattering (MALS) and refractive index detection (RID) is the current gold standard.4 This multi-detector configuration bypasses the need for arbitrary calibration standards by utilizing the fundamental physics of light scattering to determine absolute molar mass directly. In plant protein systems undergoing intensive Maillard-induced conjugation, HPSEC-MALS-RID reveals massive architectural shifts. For instance, studies analyzing the covalent conjugation of plant proteins with carbohydrate byproducts demonstrate that unconjugated protein fractions, which originally exhibit a weight-average molar mass (![][image7]) of approximately 290 kDa and a relatively tight polydispersity index (![][image8]) of 1.35, undergo massive macromolecular expansion post-reaction.21 The resulting cross-linked melanoidin-protein complexes show an extreme shift in ![][image7], ranging from 340 to 359 kDa, alongside a broadened polydispersity index of 1.74, indicative of the heterogeneous nature of the polymerization process.21  
Furthermore, HPSEC-MALS provides exact quantitative data on the physical dimensions and compactness of the polymer coils in solution. The z-average root-mean-square radius of gyration (![][image9]) of these complexes has been shown to increase from 29.5 nm in the native state to between 30.5 and 33.5 nm following melanoidin conjugation, confirming the literal physical expansion of the covalently aggregated network.21 Crucially, the Mark-Houwink exponent 'a'—a parameter derived from intrinsic viscosity measurements that describes the conformation of the polymer chain—demonstrates a significant reduction from 0.53 to 0.40.21 In polymer physics, an 'a' value approaching 0.5 suggests a flexible, random coil in a theta solvent, whereas a drop toward 0.3 or 0.4 indicates the formation of a highly branched, dense, and tightly compacted spherical structure. This quantitative drop in the Mark-Houwink exponent definitively proves that the melanoidin-driven cross-linking forces the extruded plant proteins into a significantly denser and more compact conformation than their native counterparts.21  
When advanced chromatography or radiolabeling is unavailable, specific colorimetric calibrations can still yield absolute concentration values if properly standardized. The absolute concentration of melanoidins (![][image10], in mg/mL) in extracted solutions can be mathematically derived using a predefined standard curve:

Where ![][image12] is the absorbance at 470 nm, ![][image13] is the total fixed volume of the solution, ![][image14] is the original sample volume, and the constant 0.269 represents the experimentally determined specific absorbance of exactly 0.1 mg of isolated standard melanoidins in a 1.0 mL aqueous solution.22 Additionally, Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionization Mass Spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) is frequently employed to profile the precise mass of the individual protein subunits participating in the cross-linking, successfully identifying major plant globulin fractions ranging from 10.5 to 52.2 kDa that serve as the primary scaffolds for melanoidin attachment.23

## **Macromolecular Architecture and Covalent Cross-Linking Dynamics**

The generation of high-molecular-weight melanoidins does not occur in chemical isolation; it is inextricably linked to the physical texturization and spatial phase transitions of the plant protein matrix within the extruder. The specific botanical origin of the protein—whether soy or pea—fundamentally dictates the architectural evolution of the extrudate, as the amino acid profiles and globulin ratios determine the matrix's capacity for covalent cross-linking.  
Soy protein isolate is exceptionally reactive. It contains the 11S glycinin and 7S ![][image1]\-conglycinin fractions, which are rich in sulfur-containing amino acids and highly susceptible to thermal unfolding. Pea protein isolate, conversely, is dominated by legumin and vicilin fractions, which exhibit different isoelectric properties and a generally lower baseline solubility.4 During HME, both isolates undergo profound physical degradation, but their distinct chemistries lead to highly divergent macroscopic architectures.  
To quantify the extent of covalent cross-linking occurring during extrusion, researchers employ protein extraction protocols utilizing increasingly harsh solvent systems. Extractions utilizing severe denaturing and reducing agents—specifically combinations of urea, dithiothreitol (DTT), and sodium dodecyl sulphate (SDS)—are used to dismantle non-covalent interactions (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions) and reducible covalent bonds (disulfide bridges). Analyses utilizing these severe solvents reveal a marked 5–10% absolute decrease in extractable proteins for both SPI and PPI extrudates compared to their raw, unextruded native powders.26 This reduction in extractability is a direct quantitative indicator of the formation of massive, entirely insoluble, non-reducible covalent aggregates.27 These super-aggregates are stabilized by the irreversible Maillard-derived isopeptide bonds and the bulky HMW melanoidin cross-links that act as permanent bridges between individual protein chains.27  
The macroscopic architecture of the extrudate is heavily influenced by these competing cross-linking pathways. SPI demonstrates an exceptionally high inherent cross-linking potential under thermal shear. It generally requires a lower specific mechanical energy (SME) threshold to initiate texturization, ultimately resulting in a denser, compact, gel-like structure with high internal porosity but less pronounced macroscopic layering.26 Conversely, PPI concentrates and isolates, which have a lower propensity for rapid disulfide bridging, generally produce structures that are distinctly layered and highly anisotropic, mimicking the distinct bundle structures of animal muscle.26  
Spectroscopic investigations into the secondary structures of these matrices using Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) provide mechanistic insight into how the physical strain and chemical cross-linking alter the foundational hydrogen-bonding networks of the proteins. In commercial PPI, the proportion of random coil configurations significantly increases from 14.04% to 19.36% immediately following extrusion.27 This significant architectural shift indicates a forced, permanent disruption of native ![][image3]\-helices and ordered ![][image1]\-sheets. The protein backbone is forced to adopt extended, disordered random coil conformations to physically accommodate the immense steric hindrance introduced by the formation of bulky melanoidin adducts and extensive intermolecular cross-linking.27  
The presence of melanoidins within this matrix functions as an in-situ generated thermosetting resin.10 As the internal barrel temperature of the extruder escalates—often traversing distinct heating zones of 60, 90, 110, and 120 °C—the molecular weight and cross-link density of the forming melanoidins increase simultaneously.1 These complex polymers facilitate powerful interparticle bonding, effectively locking the highly plasticized, flowing protein chains into a fixed, irreversible conformation the moment the melt enters the cooling die. Once this dense cross-linked network is established, it heavily resists subsequent thermal disruption.

| Matrix Characteristic | Soy Protein Isolate (SPI) Extrudate | Pea Protein Isolate (PPI) Extrudate |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **SME Requirement for Texturization** | Relatively low; rapid and highly reactive cross-linking | Moderate to high; heavily dependent on feed moisture |
| **Macroscopic Internal Architecture** | Porous, compact continuous gel, less pronounced layering | Distinctly layered, highly anisotropic fibrous bundles |
| **Extractability Reduction (Urea/DTT/SDS)** | 5–10% decrease (formation of non-reducible aggregates) | 5–10% decrease (formation of non-reducible aggregates) |
| **Primary Covalent Stabilization** | High S-S disulfide bonding and melanoidin bridging | Moderate S-S bonding, dominant hydrogen and melanoidin bonding |
| **Secondary Structure Shifts (FTIR)** | Minimal macroscopic changes detected overall | Significant structural disorder; random coils increase to 19.36% |

## **Rheological Phase Transitions and Macroscopic Physical Impacts**

The microscopic covalent linkages forged by melanoidin polymers and disulfide bonds scale up directly to dictate the macroscopic rheology, elasticity, and hydration kinetics of the extruded matrix. The thermodynamic history of the polymer network permanently sets its physical limits, dictating critical commercial metrics such as Water Holding Capacity (WHC), Water Solubility Index (WSI), and overall mechanical elasticity.  
The increasingly rigid nature of the melanoidin-cross-linked network physically restricts the swelling capacity of the protein matrix, fundamentally altering how the polymer interacts with solvent water. The permanence of these thermomechanical changes is best illustrated through rework studies, where previously extruded materials are dried, milled, and subjected to a subsequent extrusion cycle. A single HME cycle violently reduces the solubility of the raw isolates, dropping it by 15% for PPI and a severe 74% for SPI.9 Correspondingly, the WHC is reduced by 17% for SPI and a staggering 65% for PPI.9 This extreme drop corresponds to the dense packing of the protein molecules and the profound hydrophobicity introduced by the melanoidin cross-links, which physically exclude water from infiltrating the polymer network.  
When the material is freeze-dried, ground, and forced through a second HME cycle, the hydration capacity is nearly obliterated. Following this second cycle, the reduction in WHC plummets further to 63% for SPI and an extreme 90% reduction for PPI compared to the native, unextruded isolates.9 Similarly, the absolute solubility drops to 22% for PPI and 79% for SPI.9 Despite this extreme loss of hydration capacity, advanced rheological evaluations measuring the storage modulus (![][image15]) and loss modulus (![][image16]) indicate that the internal structural integrity of the polymer melt remains remarkably intact. The anisotropic indices and cutting strengths of SPI extrudates demonstrate virtually no significant degradation even after two full extrusion cycles, providing definitive proof that the established covalent melanoidin network is virtually immune to subsequent thermomechanical melting or disruption.9  
To mathematically quantify the viscoelastic phase transitions of these heavily cross-linked plant proteins, advanced non-linear rheological models must be utilized. The mechanical firmness of the final extrudates—which can range widely from 10 N to 104 N depending on specific feed moisture levels (typically optimized between 20% and 30%) and the exact ratios of protein isolates—is a direct functional output of the cross-link density established by the Maillard reaction.1 To express the mathematical relationship between the compression stress applied to the extrudate and the physical deformation of these robust, rubber-like protein gels, the first-order Ogden model is frequently applied:  
![][image17]  
Within this equation, ![][image18] represents the true compressive stress, ![][image19] represents the principal stretch ratio (the degree of deformation), ![][image3] is the strain hardening exponent related directly to the non-linear elasticity of the cross-linked network, and ![][image20] represents the foundational shear modulus of the material in its reference state.30 The extensive generation of melanoidin complexes fundamentally alters this equation by increasing the effective shear modulus (![][image20]). The melanoidins act as highly rigid, covalently bound filler particles dispersed throughout the continuous protein phase, increasing the strain hardening exponent and rendering the matrix highly resistant to compressive failure.  
Furthermore, the continuous generation of these polymers drastically impacts the flow behavior of the plasticized protein melt as it traverses the active cooking zones of the extruder barrel. The dimensionless Trouton ratio (![][image21]), which compares the relative magnitude of extensional viscosity to shear viscosity, is utilized to characterize the deformation of the melt.31 As the Maillard reaction rapidly consumes available basic amino acids like lysine and arginine, the net electrical charge and isoelectric properties of the melt shift. This reduces electrostatic repulsion between adjacent protein chains, promoting premature aggregation and significantly increasing the apparent viscosity and the storage modulus (![][image15]). The rheology of this reactive melt is highly non-Newtonian and is typically characterized utilizing Power Law, Casson, or Bingham plastic models, requiring continuous computational adjustments to screw speed and torque to maintain uniform laminar flow through the die.32

## **Volatile Thiol Scavenging: The Quantitative Binding Capacity of Melanoidins**

Perhaps the most consequential, yet historically under-appreciated, physical impact of HMW melanoidin formation in extruded plant proteins is their profound and aggressive binding capacity for small volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Extruded plant-based matrices—such as TVP and high-moisture meat analogues—inherently lack the complex, savory aromatic profiles of actual animal muscle. Consequently, they require the exogenous addition of potent flavoring agents to mask inherent "beany" off-notes derived from lipid oxidation (e.g., hexanal) and to accurately simulate the aromatic profile of cooked meat.35 However, a severe physicochemical paradox exists within this process: the exact covalent melanoidin networks required to provide desirable, meat-like anisotropic textures actively scavenge, bind, and neutralize the key odorants required to provide meat-like flavor.  
The most critical of these flavor compounds are volatile sulfur-containing thiols, specifically 2-methyl-3-furanthiol (MFT) and its homologue 2-furfurylthiol (FFT).35 MFT is a highly potent flavor molecule generated primarily through the Maillard reaction between carbohydrates and cysteine, or through the thermal degradation of thiamine.12 It possesses an intensely powerful meaty, sweet, and sulfurous aroma, exhibiting exceptionally low human sensory detection thresholds. In water, MFT can be detected at mere concentrations of 0.007 ![][image22]g/kg, and in the air at 0.0025 ng/L.12  
Under the extreme high-heat conditions of extrusion, flavor compounds containing free sulfhydryl (-SH) groups undergo rapid degradation or matrix binding. While a fraction of this loss is attributable to simple thermal oxidation into inactive disulfides, the predominant, overwhelming mechanism for the depletion of MFT in Maillard-rich environments is direct covalent conjugation to the HMW melanoidin skeleton.11  
The mechanistic chemical pathway for this extreme binding capacity is driven by highly reactive radical intermediates generated during the intermediate stages of the Maillard cascade. Specifically, compounds known as CROSSPY-type radicals—formally identified as 1,4-bis-(5-amino-5-carboxy-1-pentyl)pyrazinium radical cations—serve as the primary, aggressive reactive sites embedded along the growing melanoidin polymer chain.11 When MFT or FFT comes into contact with these pyrazinium intermediates, the free thiol group undergoes an irreversible redox coupling reaction. This results in the formation of highly stable, non-volatile thioether adducts.12 This covalent tethering permanently removes the thiol from the volatile headspace, severely diminishing the macroscopic sensory perception of the extrudate, rendering it aromatically flat.12  
Rigorous quantitative assessments of this binding capacity reveal the extreme efficiency of melanoidins as permanent flavor sinks. Advanced analytical techniques utilizing stable isotope dilution assays (SIDA) paired with headspace gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) have precisely mapped the depletion parameters of these thiols.12 When standardized volatile thiol fractions are exposed to isolated HMW melanoidins (mass \> 3000 Da), the relative flavor dilution (rFD) factor of MFT demonstrates a catastrophic drop.12 In controlled aqueous models designed to simulate the thermal history of Maillard-heavy matrices, the presence of just 125 mg of isolated HMW melanoidins was sufficient to reduce the rFD factor of MFT from 4 down to 2, effectively halving the perceived aromatic intensity at the threshold level.12  
Furthermore, absolute concentration measurements reveal that homologous thiols like 2-furfurylthiol decrease by an extreme factor of 16 immediately upon interaction with a saturated melanoidin matrix.11 To parameterize this capacity mathematically, researchers utilize the half-maximal binding capacity (![][image23]). This metric calculates the exact mass of volatile thiol required to saturate 50% of the available active pyrazinium sites within a specified volume of a standardized Maillard polymer matrix. Experimental data yield a highly significant ![][image23] value of 183 mg of thiol per liter of melanoidin-rich standard solution.38

| Volatile Thiol Binding Metric | Measured Quantitative Value | Direct Implication for Extruded Plant Matrices |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Absolute Thiol Concentration Drop** | Decreased by a factor of 16 | Rapid, near-total depletion of added meaty flavors post-extrusion. |
| **Relative Flavor Dilution (rFD) Factor** | Reduced from 4 to 2 (with 125mg isolated melanoidin) | 50% loss in threshold detection intensity; requires massive flavor over-dosing. |
| **Half-Maximal Binding Capacity (![][image23])** | 183 mg thiol / L matrix | Demonstrates the massive innate capacity of melanoidins to trap volatile sulfur compounds. |
| **Primary Covalent Binding Mechanism** | Thioether formation via CROSSPY radical cations | Irreversible covalent binding; the trapped flavor cannot be released upon mastication or heating. |

These precise quantitative metrics present a profound thermodynamic and commercial contradiction at the very heart of plant protein texturization: the exact thermal parameters (high SME, high temperature, low moisture) that are strictly necessary to generate the covalent melanoidin cross-links required for optimal anisotropic texture simultaneously maximize the concentration of CROSSPY radical sites. This creates an internal chemical environment that is fundamentally hostile to the retention of sulfur-based flavors, presenting a major barrier to the organoleptic success of plant-based meat analogues.

## **Mathematical Modeling of Extrusion-Induced Polymerization**

Predicting the precise extent of Maillard precursor consumption and its direct translation into the physical topology of the protein network necessitates robust multivariate mathematical modeling. Because the consumption of basic amino acids and reducing sugars is highly sensitive to localized moisture gradients, pressure variations, and mechanical shear within the extruder, traditional linear kinetics fail to accurately predict final macroscopic physical properties such as physical lightness (![][image4]), the expansion index (EI), or hydration capacity (HC).  
For instance, the physical lightness (![][image4]) of an extrudate—often used as a direct optical marker of melanoidin accumulation—cannot be defined by a simple linear equation. This is because ![][image4] is simultaneously impacted by the inherent pigmentation of the raw protein isolates, the matrix crystallinity, the density of the cross-links, and the internal pore expansion.1 Increased covalent cross-linking creates a denser, less porous structure that traps light, lowering the ![][image4] value. Simultaneously, thermomechanical amorphous phase transitions can scatter light, raising the ![][image4] value, creating highly non-linear optical outputs that obfuscate the true extent of chemical polymerization.1  
To resolve this multi-dimensional complexity, engineers and researchers heavily employ Response Surface Methodology (RSM) utilizing Central Composite Rotatable Designs (CCRD). This statistical methodology extracts continuous mathematical relationships linking the independent processing input parameters—such as precursor concentration, feed moisture (![][image24]), barrel temperature (![][image25]), and screw speed (![][image26])—to the dependent physical output responses (![][image27]). The standard second-degree polynomial equation utilized to model these interconnected physical phase changes in extruded protein isolates is expressed as:  
![][image28]  
Where ![][image27] represents the targeted physical response (such as breaking force, storage modulus ![][image15], water solubility index, or absolute melanoidin mass), ![][image29] is the independent intercept, ![][image30] are the linear regression coefficients, ![][image31] are the quadratic coefficients defining the non-linear limits of polymerization, and ![][image32] represent the critical interaction coefficients between the highly coupled extrusion variables.1  
By utilizing this comprehensive mathematical framework, it becomes possible to optimize the extrusion environment to balance the competing demands of the matrix. For example, utilizing these models, it has been determined that optimizing the feed moisture to a narrow window of 20–25% while replacing 10–20% of the primary SPI with alternative isolates can successfully generate TVPs with a highly targeted mechanical firmness ranging from 10 N to 104 N.1 This mathematical approach allows processing engineers to precisely calibrate the input of competitive Maillard inhibitors or carefully control the thermodynamics of the melt to guarantee the necessary generation of structural melanoidins, while mitigating the excessive loss of essential lysine residues and preventing the total annihilation of flavor-binding capacity.

## **Conclusions and Systemic Trade-Offs in Plant-Based Meat Analogues**

The rigorous interrogation of thermomechanical extrusion processes in soy and pea protein isolates reveals that high-molecular-weight melanoidins are not merely passive, aesthetic byproducts of thermal degradation. Rather, they are integral, active structural elements that define both the rheological destiny and the aromatic viability of the final extrudate. The synthesis of chemical kinetics, physical rheology, and advanced analytical quantification exposes several deeply intertwined, systemic dynamics that govern plant protein texturization.  
First, the irreversible physical texturization achieved during high-moisture extrusion is fundamentally reliant on the concurrent action of protein denaturation and Maillard-induced covalent polymerization. The creation of HMW melanoidin complexes—demonstrating radically expanded molar masses up to 359 kDa, highly compacted structures evident by reduced Mark-Houwink exponents, and expansive radii of gyration—functions exactly analogously to a thermosetting resin within the protein melt. This covalent cross-linking forces a transition from native, water-soluble globular states to highly anisotropic, rigid networks. This transition is definitively evidenced by drastic shifts toward disordered secondary structures, a 5–10% reduction in absolute protein extractability, and the near-total obliteration of the matrix's native water-holding capacity, which can drop by up to 90% following multiple extrusion cycles.  
Second, the structural benefits of this cross-linking represent a profound, antagonistic trade-off with the organoleptic viability of the matrix. The accumulation of these massive melanoidin polymers inherently populates the protein matrix with highly reactive pyrazinium (CROSSPY) radical intermediates. These radical sites exhibit a voracious, aggressive chemical affinity for essential volatile thiols, boasting a staggering half-maximal binding capacity (![][image23]) of 183 mg/L. Through irreversible thioether conjugation, these melanoidins are capable of permanently neutralizing key flavor components like 2-methyl-3-furanthiol, diminishing their aromatic impact by factors of up to 16\. Consequently, the pursuit of superior anisotropic texture via extreme thermomechanical stress inherently guarantees the systematic destruction of volatile meat-like flavor profiles.  
Ultimately, mastering the texturization of plant-based protein isolates requires precise thermodynamic and mathematical control over the Maillard cascade. Future advancements in extrusion engineering must leverage non-linear rheological modeling and precise calibration of specific mechanical energy to decouple protein unfolding from advanced glycation. Only by doing so can the industry ensure that the structural integrity provided by mild melanoidin cross-linking does not trigger the catastrophic flavor-scavenging dynamics inherent to extreme high-molecular-weight polymerization, thereby resolving the central paradox of modern plant-based meat analogue production.
